key_insight: Not every item in a user's interaction history needs the same amount of computation. Most stabilize after shallow processing, while a critical minority require deeper processing to support the final recommendation.
problem_solved: Sequential recommenders typically assign a fixed computational budget to every historical item, overlooking large differences in how much processing individual items need.
method: Diagnose item-level computational needs by examining when item representations stabilize across processing depth.
Use item-level adaptive recursion to vary processing depth across items, as indicated by the paper's title.
Note: The supplied abstract is truncated, so the precise allocation mechanism and evaluation results are unavailable.
impact: Adaptive computation could help practitioners concentrate processing on items that need it rather than treating all interactions equally. The supplied excerpt does not establish measured efficiency gains or recommendation-quality improvements.
visual_elements: User-history timeline with different recursion depths assigned to individual items.
Side-by-side diagram comparing uniform processing with item-level adaptive processing.
Conceptual convergence chart showing most items stabilizing early and a minority requiring full depth.
Spotlight icon highlighting the small subset of items needing deeper computation.
paper_title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
paper_authors: Zhanshuo Cao, Jiakai Tang, Yuqi Zhou, Sunhao Dai, Jun Xu
